## Overview A digital finger strength trainer for climbers, built on the ESP32 platform with a load cell and a LilyGo T-Display S2 AMOLED. The device measures isometric finger loading in real time and spoofs the Bluetooth protocol used by the Tindeq (commercial equivalent) so it pairs with any app already compatible with that device, including frez/climbharder 2.0. ## Why it matters Traditional no-hang training uses a loading pin and a stack of weights. That setup works, but it locks you into whatever discrete weight increments you own. This device measures force continuously, so you can program precise isometric interval training and target loads within a few percent of your actual limit. That precision is the difference between progressive overload and injury. Climbing finger injuries almost always come from overreaching. Going too heavy too fast, or loading in a position the tissue isn't prepared for. Training close to your limit with accurate feedback lets you maximize progression while staying under the threshold where tendons and pulleys begin to tear. ## Demo

A pocket slide rule made from printed circuit board, combining vintage calculation methods with modern PCB manufacturing.
Initial concept sparked by the desire to combine vintage calculation methods with modern manufacturing techniques.
Deep dive into slide rule mechanics, scale calculations, and PCB manufacturing constraints. Studied historical designs and identified key features to implement.
Designing the mechanical aspects including sliding mechanisms, tolerances, and structural integrity within PCB manufacturing constraints.
Modeling a crude physical 'zeroth' prototype to validate stacked layer design and physical dimensions.
Finalizing the physical dimensions and component placement to optimize both functionality and manufacturing efficiency.
Creating the visual scale markings, numbering systems, and aesthetic elements to be silk-screened and etched to reveal the gold beneath the soldermask.
Translating the mechanical and graphic designs into manufacturable PCB files using KiCad, ensuring all tolerances and manufacturer specifications are met.
First prototype PCB manufacturing and assembly. Testing mechanical fit, scale accuracy, and overall usability. Currently working through cursor window challenges.
Optimizing the design and manufacturing process for larger scale production while maintaining quality and cost effectiveness.
Setting up supply chain, packaging design, and distribution channels for getting PCBrules to customers worldwide.
Full production launch with online sales platform, customer support, and ongoing product improvements based on user feedback.

The cursor windows sit directly on the faces of the scales, which creates increased friction when sliding, catching that moves the cursor unintentionally during calculations, and contact that risks scratching the scale surfaces over time.

Redesigning the cursor to ride on the top and bottom edges of the stator, lifting it off the scale faces entirely. Requires careful engineering of the cursor geometry and potentially adding guide rails or tracks.

Acrylic is prone to scratching with repeated use. The windows are currently the most fragile component of the assembly, and scratches on the viewing windows would significantly impact usability and scale readability long-term.

Experimenting with milled polycarbonate cursor windows. Polycarbonate offers superior impact and scratch resistance compared to acrylic, potentially making the PCBrule nearly indestructible while maintaining optical clarity.

Stainless steel shims provide clearance for the slide and cursor movement, but they are currently cut from shim strips using scissors. Extremely crude, painstaking, unrepeatable, and prone to shifting or falling out.
Purchased a 2mm hole punch to use in conjunction with a 3D-printed jig to quickly, accurately, and repeatably produce the small stainless steel shims.

## Story I was a freshman in high school when I first learned what a slide rule was. My FIRST robotics mentor brought a slide rule to a meeting one day and I was blown away by the magic math stick and what it could do. I've always been attracted to purely mechanical things — I love analog photography because I find it really neat that you can produce an image using only gears, curtains, levers, glass, and chemistry. My favorite school supply throughout high school was a cherry red DigiKey PCB ruler — there was a satisfying quality about the gold lettering and just how durable it was. Since then, I've had a nagging idea in my head: *"Wouldn't it be awesome if you made a slide rule out of Printed Circuit Board?"* Now as a student in university I am finally acting on that idea — and it is pretty awesome in my opinion. ## Inspiration "If you've had this idea for a while, what pushed you to actually make it?" you ask. Well it's simple. I am a student in a competitive field. I wanted to make a really cool and memorable "business card" that I could hand out at my school's career fair. I was hoping this memorable object would sit on a company recruiter's desk with my name on it, and they'd see it, and give me an internship. Selling them and bringing it to market was mostly an afterthought. ![PCBrule panel layout](/images/pcbrule/panel.jpg) ## Wait, what's a slide rule? A slide rule is a mechanical calculator — engineers used them before the advent of digital computers. It is a tool that operates on the principle of adding together logarithms. The Apollo astronauts carried a Pickett N600-ES to the moon, and the PCBrule is modeled after that very same design — with identical scales and calculation capabilities. Its layout has been time tested and literally approved by NASA. ## Current Prototype Demonstration

Designed a mechanical fin attachment system for Project Kline's subscale vehicle, cutting fin replacement time from 24+ hours to a 30-minute hot-swap.

## The problem

Last University Student Launch Initiative (USLI) season, I was tasked with researching and developing a mechanical fin attachment system for the Project Kline subscale vehicle.

In previous seasons, there had been issues with repeated fin damage and breakage after flights. This problem had to be fixed by grinding, filing, and sanding down the epoxy fillets before reattaching the replacement fins — a painful, exhausting, and hazardous 24+ hour process.

To combat this, the team decided to research a mechanical fin attachment system.

## The solution

The solution I came up with (pictured above) proved to be extremely helpful on the subscale vehicle, as the team experimented with different fin shapes that could be hot-swapped within a 30-minute window at the launch site.

## Outcome and trade-offs

Ultimately, while the system was useful on the subscale vehicle for testing and validating fin designs, the team chose to return to traditional epoxy bonded fins for the full-scale rocket. The decision favored flight vehicle mass savings and decreased complexity, at the cost of increased fin replacement time and labor.

## What I learned

- **Mechanical design under real constraints** — tolerances, retention, and thermal/structural loads all had to work together in a system that could be assembled and disassembled repeatedly without degradation.
- **Design for manufacturing and field use** — a design that works on a bench but takes an hour to install at a launch site isn't useful. The 30-minute hot-swap target shaped every decision.
- **Engineering trade-offs** — the mechanical system won on iteration speed and lost on mass. Recognizing when the trade-off favors the simpler solution is as important as building the complex one.

DIY Snowskate from a Kids' Ski
Built a functional snowskate from a thrifted kids' ski, a plastic skateboard deck, and waterjet-cut aluminum trucks I designed in CAD.

## The build I built this snowskate from a kids' ski I thrifted and a plastic skateboard deck. The interface between the two, a pair of rocker mounting trucks I designed in CAD specifically for waterjet cutting. The design had to solve a few problems at once: - **Match two curved surfaces.** A ski is cambered; a skateboard deck is flat. The mounting plates had to bridge that gap without introducing stress concentrations that would crack the plastic deck. I drew inspiration from a pivot and rocker style design. The front truck pivots only where it meets the ski. The rear truck has pivots on both the deck side and the ski side. This three bar pivot mechanism allows the ski to flex under the weight of the rider and to bend arround depresions and hills in the terrain. Carving charecteristics on skis and snowboards require the weight of the skier or boarder to bend the ski against the camber until the edge contacts the point along a single curve. - **Survive impact.** Snowskates take a beating, hard landings, rail hits, icy patches. Everything had to be overbuilt enough to handle that. Using oil-impregnated bronze bushings in the pivots allowed me to acvhieve tight tolerances with nearly no slop or play in the pivots, which allowed rider feedback and controll authority to transmit though the trucks and into the ski. - **Be manufacturable in one pass.** Waterjet is a 2D process. Every feature from mounting holes, and contours had to fit on a flat sheet. ## Learning to ride it
I had so much fun learning how to ride this thing, falling on my butt many times but getting back on. By the end of the first trip I got the hang of it and was able to get on and ride off the chairlift. Once you understand the balance and weight distribution, it behaves a lot like a snowboard. The foot placement is narrower and the platform is shorter, so the response is twitchier, but the fundamentals are the same in terms of edge controll, weight balance, and turn commitment. ## What I learned - **Design for a specific process.** Waterjet is subtractive 2D I wanted to add waterjet cutting to my list of familiar fabrication methods. Drawing inspiration from traditional no-glue woodworking techniques, I used a tenon and mortise style joint for rigidity. - **Physical prototyping teaches faster than simulation.** I had no idea if this would even be ridable, I asked the snowskate community on Reddit but they seemed pretty sure that my ski was going to be too short and narrow to ride. Already having the ski and the parts, I decided to pull the trigger and it turned out to be a lot of fun. - **Iteration through failure.** Every fall was feedback. By the end of the first trip, my balance had adapted to the platform, that wouldn't have happened without committing to ride it badly for a few hours first.

Mechanical Engineering Student's Every Day Carry
A repurposed camera filter pouch rebuilt into a modular tool roll that carries a full field repair kit in the water bottle pocket of a backpack.
Identified a camera filter pouch as a candidate housing, mapped out the contents I needed to carry, and planned the modification layout.
Removed four mesh pockets, sewed waistband elastic to retain the tools, and added two Tyvek flaps cut from a USPS mailer to keep everything contained in transport.

Added scissors and a carpenter pencil after initial use. Coordinating the pouch with a separate car kit (impact driver, sockets, consumables) so the full system covers on-the-go repairs without duplicating weight.

## Overview A tool roll built from a repurposed camera filter pouch. The original pouch had mesh pockets that couldn't hold small tools securely, so I removed four of them, sewed waistband elastic down the interior spine to retain drivers and hex keys, and added two Tyvek flaps cut from a USPS mailer to keep everything contained when the roll is closed and bouncing around in a bag. It's a small project, but I use it nearly every day. Every tool in it has been picked because it solves a problem I've actually run into. 3d printer fixes, slide rule assembly, climbing hold tightening, pulling out nails from the walls in my role as asistant art curator, epoxying together the cracked base of my camera. It carries enough to handle most field problems without turning into a full toolbox. Curate and install rotating art exhibitions across campus spaces, working with faculty to align placement with community needs and provide recognition for emerging local artists.

Two years leading the Rose-Hulman climbing team with one goal: build climbers who keep climbing for life, not just for a competition season.

## Overview

Managed the Rose-Hulman climbing team for two seasons with a single guiding goal: build climbers who keep climbing for the rest of their lives. Competition results matter, but they're not the point, the point is that when someone graduates, they leave with a sport they love, a community they belong to, and the skills to keep progressing on their own.

## The philosophy

The collegiate climbing circuit is a strange environment. It rewards a small slice of the team for a short window of time, and then everyone graduates and most people quit. I wanted to build something that outlasted the season, a team that served climbers regardless of whether they wanted to compete, and that sent people into the world with climbing as a lifelong practice.

That meant running a program that treated competitive ambition as one goal among many, not the goal itself. Some climbers trained for Nationals; some just wanted to get stronger for outdoor trips; some came for the community and competed as an afterthought. All of those were legitimate outcomes.

## Goal-based training

I built individual training plans for each climber on the roster, anchored to their own stated goal rather than a team-wide program. The structure looked different for everyone. A periodized competition block for one climber, a general strength and technique block for another, and a lighter schedule for someone balancing climbing against a heavy academic term.

## What I did

- **Individualized training plans** — built goal-based programs for each climber, anchored to specific benchmarks rather than open-ended improvement
- **Frequent testing** — ran regular assessments to measure progress, using the data to adjust training blocks rather than collecting it without action
- **Weekly team workouts** — ran structured sessions at the Rose-Hulman wall that served every level of the roster
- **Trips** — organized paid team trips to Indianapolis gyms and free club trips, giving climbers training opportunities outside the campus wall and a reason to spend time together outside of practice
- **Competition support** — qualified 2 climbers to Nationals in the 2024 season and 4 in the 2025 season, with two first-place finishes and overall 3rd place team ranking in 2024 and an individual placement of 4th in 2025
- **Travel logistics** — planned and budgeted team travel, coordinating transportation, lodging, and competition registration
- **Inclusivity** — built a program where competitive and recreational climbers both had a place, without diluting either experience

Advised customers on outdoor gear selection using firsthand climbing and camping experience, while managing returns and customer-service escalations.

## Overview

Frontline sales and camp/climb associate, advising customers on gear selection across climbing, camping, and outdoor categories. Used personal climbing and camping experience to recommend products that fit specific use cases rather than pushing whatever was on the shelf.

## What I did

- **Product guidance** — helped customers select climbing and camping gear based on their actual experience level, intended use, and budget — recommending less expensive options when they were better suited, and upselling only when it was justified
- **Specialty category expertise** — served as a camp and climb specialist, handling technical questions about harnesses, ropes, protection, and camping systems
- **Customer service** — handled returns, exchanges, and dissatisfied customers, learning to defuse tense conversations by listening first and solving the actual problem rather than defending policy
- **Frontline operations** — restocked, ran register, and supported the sales floor during peak weekend hours

## What I learned

How to have a real conversation with someone who's frustrated — a return, a broken piece of gear, an expectation that wasn't met — without becoming defensive or defaulting to policy. Listening first, asking what outcome would actually solve their problem, and then working within what's possible usually gets further than arguing. It's the same skill as explaining a technical trade-off to a stakeholder who disagrees: figure out what they actually need before deciding what to say.

Overview

Frontline sales and camp/climb associate, advising customers on gear selection across climbing, camping, and outdoor categories. Used personal climbing and camping experience to recommend products that fit specific use cases rather than pushing whatever was on the shelf.

What I did

  • Product guidance — helped customers select climbing and camping gear based on their actual experience level, intended use, and budget — recommending less expensive options when they were better suited, and upselling only when it was justified
  • Specialty category expertise — served as a camp and climb specialist, handling technical questions about harnesses, ropes, protection, and camping systems
  • Customer service — handled returns, exchanges, and dissatisfied customers, learning to defuse tense conversations by listening first and solving the actual problem rather than defending policy
  • Frontline operations — restocked, ran register, and supported the sales floor during peak weekend hours

What I learned

How to have a real conversation with someone who’s frustrated — a return, a broken piece of gear, an expectation that wasn’t met — without becoming defensive or defaulting to policy. Listening first, asking what outcome would actually solve their problem, and then working within what’s possible usually gets further than arguing. It’s the same skill as explaining a technical trade-off to a stakeholder who disagrees: figure out what they actually need before deciding what to say.
Designed and set climbing routes applying biomechanics, spatial reasoning, and safety principles.

## Overview

Routesetting is a blend of spatial design, biomechanics, and communication. Each route is a puzzle, you design movement sequences that challenge climbers at a specific difficulty grade while remaining safe and fair.

## Skills demonstrated

- **Biomechanics** — understanding how body positioning, reach, and leverage affect difficulty
- **Spatial reasoning** — visualizing 3D movement on a 2D wall layout
- **Safety** — ensuring routes are settable and climbable without unnecessary risk
- **Communication** — explaining route beta and adjusting based on climber feedback

## What I learned

How to design for a diverse range of body types and skill levels, and why iteration matters in physical design.

Led youth climbing camp programming at Sender One Aliso Viejo, managing daily operations, instruction, and parent communication for groups of young climbers.

## Overview

Led summer camp programming at Sender One Aliso Viejo, running daily climbing sessions for youth groups. Responsible for instruction, safety, group management, and the parent-facing side of the camp, progress updates, scheduling questions, and day-to-day concerns.

## What I did

- **Instruction** — taught climbing technique, movement fundamentals, and safety practices to campers across a range of ages and experience levels
- **Programming** — planned and ran daily camp schedules balancing skill instruction, climbing time, games, and rest
- **Group management** — kept groups of kids engaged, safe, and moving through multi-hour sessions
- **Parent communication** — managed expectations around progress, behavior, scheduling, and safety questions
- **Safety oversight** — enforced gym rules, checked harnesses and knots, and managed risk throughout each session

## What I learned

How to read a room and adjust in real time, a group that's losing focus needs a different approach than a group that's frustrated by a hard route. Communicating with parents taught me to translate technical progress into plain language, which is the same skill as explaining an engineering decision to a non-technical stakeholder. Both are about building trust through clarity.

Led a rebuild of the Sage Hill robotics team from 4 members to over 40, managed a $19,000 budget, and guided the team to a top-8 regional finish.

## Overview

Took over as Team Captain of an FRC team that had been reduced to 4 members by the COVID-19 pandemic and rebuilt it into a 40+ member program. Responsible for recruiting, team structure, budget, and competition strategy.

## What I did

- **Rebuilt the team** — recruited from 4 members to over 40, introducing 60+ Sage Hill students to engineering fields through outreach and programming
- **Competition results** — guided the team to an 8th of 48 placement at the Orange County Regional
- **Budget management** — managed a $19,000 operating budget, overseeing accounting and finance for parts, registration, travel, and tooling
- **Project management** — implemented workflow and coordination systems to keep a 40-person team synchronized through build season
- **Cross-team collaboration** — worked directly with teammates across mechanical, electrical, and software subteams to coordinate integration

## Prior role — Design Lead

Before becoming Captain, served as Design Lead from August 2020 to August 2023. Mentored a group of 2–6 members, developed the team's solution-seeking workflow, and applied a creative design ethos within the team's manufacturing constraints, often identifying workarounds when the ideal part wasn't available or buildable.

## What I learned

How to build something from almost nothing. Going from 4 members to 40 required recruiting, retention, and rebuilding a culture that had been disrupted by the pandemic — none of which is an engineering problem. Managing $19,000 taught me how to allocate resources against competing priorities, which turns out to be the same skill as managing a design budget under load constraints.
